extracted.intended_audience: amateur photographers, instrument makers, and general readers interested in stereoscopy and binocular vision
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and historical guidance on constructing, adjusting, and using stereoscopes and stereographs (how to prepare conjugate pictures, instrument features to avoid artifacts, and comfortable viewing technique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereographic interval / picture center spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: If two similar pictures are placed close in front of the eyes, the distance between their centers being equal to the distance between the pupils, they at once appear to coalesce into a single picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stereographic interval should roughly match the observer's interpupillary distance (about 2.5 inches average). On ordinary stereographs three inches is the usual limit; semi-lenses or optical adjustments can permit somewhat larger intervals. Mis‑spacing produces poor fusion or distracting side‑images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence and alignment of conjugate pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjugate pictures must be prepared and mounted so that corresponding horizontal lines are on the same level and the two pictures are true conjugates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wheatstone's instructions emphasize that pictures be fixed so corresponding horizontals are level. Accurate conjugacy is easiest achieved by photography rather than freehand drawing; misalignment prevents comfortable fusion and correct depth perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination or management of side‑images
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of uncombined images at the sides of the binocular picture is confusing and distracts attention; instrument design should prevent an eye from receiving the picture intended for the other eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid side‑images by using tubes/boxes (Wheatstone, Elliot), oblique mirrors (Wheatstone's reflecting stereoscope), partitions, or properly placed semi‑lenses. Side‑images are an anti‑pattern in viewing—they divert attention from the fused central image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper eye positioning and image coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer must place the eyes appropriately (e.g., near the mirrors or eye‑pieces) and adjust sliding panels/controls so the two reflected images coincide at the intersection of the optic axes and form an image of the same apparent magnitude as each component picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow instrument‑specific positioning: right eye before right mirror/eye‑piece and left before left. Adjust sliding panels, screws, or slides until images coincide. Failure to position eyes or adjust panels causes double vision or incorrect scale of the fused image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred visual alignment (parallel/slight divergence vs strong convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereoscopic vision is often easier when the visual lines are parallel or very slightly divergent rather than strongly convergent; diagrams that assume intersection of visual lines in front can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and use stereoscopes to allow relaxed (parallel or slightly divergent) viewing postures. Forcing strong convergence is uncomfortable and not necessary for stereoscopic perception; many people find parallel/distant fixation less tiring and more successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comfort and avoidance of muscular strain
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereoscopic viewing can be tiring or impossible for some observers; comfortable instruments and viewing techniques minimize ocular strain and may require muscular training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stereoscopy causes strain (sensations of pulling), give the eyes rest and practice voluntary control. Good instrument design (adjustable eye‑pieces, proper spacing, semi‑lenses) reduces fatigue. Recognize that prolonged or poorly adjusted stereoscopic viewing is wearying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument adjustability and fit to individual observers
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective stereoscope should allow adjustment for card distance and interpupillary spacing (e.g., sliding panels, draw‑out semi‑lenses, lateral motion via screws); absence of adjustment is a defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices with fixed semi‑lenses or no means to change card distance/eye separation are objectionable because they cannot be adapted to different observers or stereograph sizes. Preferred designs include screws, sliding plates, or movable tubes for fine tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical magnification and lens design
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of plano‑convex lenses or semi‑lenses (as in Brewster and Helmholtz instruments) can magnify pictures and facilitate binocular viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well‑designed lens elements (semi‑lenses, telescope‑like eyepieces) increase apparent picture size and comfort. Helmholtz‑style instruments use accurately centered plano‑convex lenses or eyepieces; cheap or incorrectly centered optics reduce image quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a binocular camera for synchronized stereographs
rubrics_metrics.description: A binocular camera with two lens combinations a few inches apart is necessary to take two pictures simultaneously from slightly different standpoints, especially for living or moving subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without simultaneous capture, moving subjects (people, clouds) may change between exposures and ruin conjugacy; the binocular camera avoids this. When photographing stereographs, two synchronized optical paths are recommended for fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic preparation preferred for accuracy of conjugate pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Photography produces highly accurate conjugate pictures for stereoscopy; without photography, freehand drawing makes perfect conjugacy impractical in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early stereoscopic practice struggled before photography; collodion & later methods enabled practical, accurate stereographs. Prefer photographic methods when exact correspondence is required (e.g., fine detail, living subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereograph size must suit instrument design
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stereoscope designs (e.g., Helmholtz with telescope eyepieces) require comparatively small stereographs to avoid optic divergence and to permit comfortable viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stereograph size appropriate to the chosen instrument. Large stereographs may be uncomfortable or incompatible with instruments that expect close card placement or certain optical geometries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic viewing conditions (lighting and framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stereoscope can simulate a sunlit scene by inserting an oblique plate with elliptical openings and using reflected gilt paper (the 'Claude Lorraine' effect) or diffused/transmitted light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To increase naturalness and aesthetic appeal, add a gilt window‑plate, diffusing glass, or adjustable hood. These are design choices to enhance perceived realism but do not replace correct optical alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, portability, strength, and low cost as virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: A good domestic stereoscope should be simple, strong, cheap, handy, and not cumbersome—qualities praised in Holmes's handheld design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instruments for general use should favor compactness and affordability while retaining necessary adjustability. Overly cumbersome or expensive designs may be less widely adopted despite optical merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unwieldy or inconvenient forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some early instruments (e.g., Wheatstone's reflecting stereoscope) were unwieldy and inconvenient compared with later, more compact devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should balance optical performance with user convenience; an otherwise good optical principle may fail in practice if the instrument is too awkward to use regularly.
